issues.legal_issue: A fictitious or fraudulent revenue-record entry cannot confer the statutory occupancy status that would otherwise follow from being recorded as an occupant on the relevant date.
material_facts: The respondents were recorded as occupants of the disputed plots in the revenue records for the relevant year.

The appellants alleged that the entry supporting the respondents’ claimed rights was fictitious, and the respondents admitted in a compromise that the entry was fictitious and that they had no interest in the property.
The consolidation authorities treated the statutory effect of the recorded entry as controlling despite the admission; the High Court upheld that approach.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s view was not good law: where evidence shows that the entry was fictitious or was made surreptitiously or fraudulently, the person named in it cannot claim the statutory occupancy status on the basis of that entry. The matter was remanded for a fresh decision.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 20(b) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, the relevant revenue-record entry is ordinarily material to the claimed status. Applying Sonavati v. Sri Ram, the Court recognized an exception where evidence shows that the entry was fictitious, surreptitious, or fraudulent. The contrary approach in Hukam Singh v. Board of Revenue was no longer good law. The claimed status mattered because Section 240(a) could affect the recorded landholders’ rights if the respondents had acquired it.

predicates.consolidation_rights_proceeding: The dispute concerns the determination of land rights in a consolidation proceeding.
predicates.occupant_recorded_on_relevant_date: A person was recorded as an occupant in the revenue records for the date relevant to the claimed statutory status.
predicates.evidence_shows_entry_fictitious_or_fraud: Evidence shows that the occupant entry was fictitious or was made surreptitiously or fraudulently.

issues.definition: When a consolidation proceeding concerns a person recorded as an occupant on the relevant date, evidence that the entry was fictitious or fraudulent means the person cannot acquire occupancy status through that entry.

issues.legal_issue: An appeal does not abate merely because one legal representative of a deceased respondent has not yet been impleaded when other legal representatives are already on the record and the omitted representative can be added.
material_facts: A respondent died while the appeal was pending.
Two of the deceased respondent’s daughters had already been impleaded as legal representatives.
A third daughter had not been impleaded earlier because information about her was not available in time, and the appellants applied to add her.
The contesting respondents objected that the appeal had abated because the third daughter had not been impleaded in time.
issues.conclusion: The appeal could not be dismissed as having abated for failure to implead the third legal representative in time; she could be added to the record.
issues.legal_principle: Where some legal representatives of a deceased party are already on the record, another legal representative can be brought on the record. On these facts, the omission did not require dismissal of the appeal as abated.

predicates.appeal_with_deceased_respondent: An appeal is pending and a respondent dies during its pendency.
predicates.some_legal_representatives_already_on_re: At least some of the deceased respondent’s legal representatives have been impleaded in the appeal.
predicates.omitted_legal_representative_can_be_adde: An omitted legal representative can be brought onto the record.

issues.definition: In an appeal involving a deceased respondent, if some legal representatives are already on the record and the omitted representative can be added, the appeal does not abate for that omission.
